How many searches are you doing that DDG shows you a rate limiting screen? It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that. Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! I feel like I was prepared for this AIrmageddon of the Web by going more and more offline. I’ve lot of physical books. I’ve relearned the trade (and the joy) of going through books to find information I’m looking for. If I realize a field is important enough for me, I buy second-hand books about the subject from before 2020. I rely more and more on official documentation and manpages. When using a library, I have more and more the reflex of checking under the hood and read the source code. It might seems daunting but, once you pass that fear, it’s extremely efficient. You don’t rely on outdated documentation: you see what you library is doing. In some case, this even allowed me to ditch the library for my own implementation when I realized that what I trully needed was a couple hundred lines of Python. For everything for which I’ve no book, no documentation, no man page, I rely mostly on Wikipedia. All those 4 points require an investment. Instead of having the right git command from stackoverflow, I skim through the official git book. It takes me 5 minutes instead of 1. It’s harder. But then, I realized something interesting: I had to go less and less for the book. I’m really building my skill, I’m learning stuff for which I was blindly relying on SO, thinking I understood stuff. Of course, not everything is offline, sadly. So: I follow a lot of interesting blogs through RSS in Offpunk (to make them offline). My only social network is Mastodon where the vast majority is against slop. I may also hang out of some good old forums/communities. I pay for Kagi as my main search engine. In the setting I’ve ask to remove IA slop. In Kagi, you can also give high/low priority to domains. I block completely domain with slops or deprioritize them. I use multiple "block slop" list in my ublock filters. If a website appears in my Kagi search but is blocked as AI slop, I ask Kagi to never show me result from this website anymore. This is far from perfect, it requires effort but this makes me a lot happier in my own personal life. This requires some sacrifices. The main problem is that it makes me live a life so different from the others that, at some point, you feel like you are not living on the same planet. I try to focus on a positive angle: the web was starting to feel awfully "corporate" and soulless even before this AI wave. Maybe the age of slop will motivate geeky communities to reinvent ourselves. And I don't just mean replacing Twitter with Mastodon or Reddit with Lobsters (I do like this place), I mean really reinventing – new networks built on top of both the internet and mesh networks, where new spaces can form. Protocols not deliberated on by committees and implemented by megacorps, but rather ad-hoc "garage" style development. Spaces that don't get swamped by "ordinary people" and the corporations that chase them (I don't at all mean to gatekeep – at least not on purpose – I simply long for organically grown communities of likeminded people on top of truly decentralized infrastructure). I only know of 3: Kagi, MetaGer, and Uruky, which I've founded with my wife and launched earlier this year exactly because we felt we needed an alternative to exist. With all of this said, I believe we really need more initiatives like EUSP (and Mojeek and Marginalia, though at different scales) which are really trying to compete with the index size of Google and Bing. Uruky allows you to use all of those and we have our own "indie/small web" index being built and it's incredibly costly to do it right, and while the big tech bots don't do it right, it's even more costly to go after them. I think it'll be by having multiple alternatives with different focuses, appealing to different kinds of uses and users.
